clue.text: He may seek asylum desperately until a ceasefire's' initiated

indicators.note: acting desperately means wildly, so the letters of the words before it are thrown into a new order
something initiated is begun, so only the start of the word ceasefire's is used

explanation.surface: A refugee keeps pressing for sanctuary until the fighting finally stops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Asylum' points to refuge, but here it is the old word for a mental hospital. 'desperately' rearranges UNTIL A into LUNATI, and 'initiated' supplies the C at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Old mental hospitals were called asylums, so a madman was the person thought to belong in one.

clue.text: Person who, around one, starts on lettuce and cucumber with lady?

definitions.text: Person who, around one, starts on lettuce and cucumber with lady?

indicators.note: around means the starting letters are placed on either side of the word for one
starts on means only the first letters of the next two words are taken

parts.note: 'un is a dialect form of one, as in 'a good 'un'
her is the pronoun for a woman

explanation.surface: Someone sits down at about one o'clock to a salad with a female companion.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken as a whole, the clue also pictures someone sitting down to a salad at lunchtime, which is why it is an all-in-one.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who eats the midday meal is a person who has lunch.

clue.text: Ballet has fool (one doing splits) and sugarplum, we hear

parts.note: a nut is a crazy or foolish person
a cracker splits shells open

indicators.note: we hear means the next word is chosen for how it sounds when spoken

parts.note: a sugarplum is a sweet

explanation.surface: A ballet features a clown doing splits and a Sugar Plum Fairy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doing splits' suggests a dancer but means a tool that cracks nuts. SWEET is said like SUITE. The Sugar Plum Fairy is a role in this ballet.
explanation.definitionFit: Tchaikovsky's orchestral suite comes from his Christmas ballet about a toy that cracks nuts.

clue.text: Frustrate, and tease endlessly about Latin composition

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so these letters are assembled in a fresh order
endlessly means the last letter of the word tease is cut off

explanation.surface: A teacher annoys a pupil by teasing them about their Latin essay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts TEASE to TEAS; 'composition' rearranges TEAS with LATIN. 'about' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Tantalus was punished with food and water just out of reach, so to tease with the unattainable is to frustrate.

clue.text: Snappy mongrel

explanation.surface: A bad-tempered dog of mixed breed.
explanation.definitionFit: A snappy mood is an irritable or angry one, and a mongrel is a mixed breed or hybrid.

clue.text: Infamous husband at university of Donnybrook?

parts.note: Mr Punch of the Punch and Judy puppet show is notorious for beating his wife
up means in residence at a university, as in 'up at Oxford'

explanation.surface: A notorious wife-beater was once a student at a Dublin college.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch and Judy is a traditional British seaside puppet show in which Punch hits his wife Judy. Donnybrook, an Irish fair notorious for brawling, gave its name to any free-for-all.
explanation.definitionFit: Donnybrook Fair near Dublin was so famous for fighting that its name came to mean any brawl.

clue.text: Leave to strip bird

parts.note: to part is to leave or go away
a ridge is a long narrow strip, as of land

explanation.surface: Permission to pluck a fowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave' reads as permission and 'strip' as plucking; they are PART and RIDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A partridge is a plump game bird.

clue.text: Relative discovers drug in French resort

indicators.note: in means the drug's letter is put inside the resort's name

parts.note: Nice is a resort on the French Riviera
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A family member is found with narcotics on the Riviera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discovers' is a link: put E in NICE.
explanation.definitionFit: A niece is the daughter of a sibling, a family member.

clue.text: Blackmailing, demanding that gold or tin be transferred in cab

indicators.note: in means the rearranged metals go inside the cab

parts.note: a hansom is a two-wheeled horse-drawn cab

indicators.note: to be transferred is to be moved about, so the letters change places

explanation.surface: A kidnapper in a taxi demands precious metal as the price of release.
explanation.walkthrough: A hansom is a Victorian horse-drawn cab. 'be transferred' rearranges the three words into OLDINGTOR; 'demanding that' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping someone captive until payment is made is extortion, much like blackmail.

clue.text: Found on pawnbroker's top shelves?

parts.note: reads as items stored high in a shop, but means things handed over as security for a loan

explanation.surface: Items kept high up in a pawnshop.
explanation.walkthrough: A pawnbroker lends money against goods left as security, kept on shelves until redeemed.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods left with a pawnbroker as security for a loan are promises of repayment.

clue.text: "Loo" entirely non-U? Ridiculous! You must be joking!

indicators.note: something ridiculous is absurd and out of order, so the letters of the quoted words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sniffs that saying 'loo' is utterly lower-class, and the listener scoffs at such snobbery.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-U was the 1950s label for words the upper classes supposedly avoided; 'loo' was in fact the U word. The fifteen letters of LOO, ENTIRELY and NONU are rearranged. 'Nellie' is rhyming slang: Nellie Duff for 'puff', breath or life.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a British idiom of flat refusal or disbelief, meaning 'not on your life'.

clue.text: Cheer for Ben as he joins the Gunners

indicators.note: the second piece is attached directly after the first, as one person joins another

parts.note: Ben-Hur is the hero of the novel and film, so Ben is followed by Hur
RA is the Royal Artillery, the British Army's gunners

explanation.surface: Applause goes up for a soldier called Ben as he enlists in the artillery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Gunners' also suggests Arsenal football club, but here it is the Royal Artillery.
explanation.definitionFit: A hurrah is a shout of joy or approval, and this is an older spelling.

clue.text: Filming an interview

explanation.surface: A camera crew records someone being questioned.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing a film on screen is a screening, and a screening is also a vetting interview that checks a candidate.

clue.text: Finally, paper slip's returned to man marked "Paid"

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word paper that follows it
returned means sent back, so the word for slip is read backwards

parts.note: a slip of paper is a small piece
Ted is a man's name, short for Edward

explanation.surface: A small paper bill comes back to a customer stamped as settled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slip' suggests a mistake or a receipt slip; it is a piece of paper, read backwards as ECEIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill that has been receipted bears a written acknowledgment that payment was made.

clue.text: Man's punishment for acquiring wisdom?

parts.note: sounds like the Fall from Eden but refers to the pain when wisdom teeth come through

explanation.surface: Humanity pays a penalty for eating from the tree of knowledge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wisdom' suggests the Garden of Eden; it means wisdom teeth, which often hurt as they erupt.
explanation.definitionFit: Wisdom teeth arrive in adulthood and often cause pain in the jaw.

clue.text: John joins you and me in spoof

indicators.note: joins means the second piece is attached straight after the first

parts.note: john is slang for a lavatory, and so is bog
you and me together make us

explanation.surface: A man named John teams up with the two of us in a hoax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John' looks like a person; it is slang for a toilet, as is British 'bog'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoof used as an adjective means fake or sham, the same as bogus.

clue.text: There's torturing 19 here

parts.note: 19 refers to that entry, the part of the leg one stands on, and the clue describes a punishment aimed at it

explanation.surface: A place where feet are tormented.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer to 19 is the foot, and the bastinado is a punishment of beating the soles of the feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Bastinado is a torture of caning the soles of the feet.

clue.text: Subject-matter consists of an article to which I object

parts.note: the is the definite article in grammar
the object form of the pronoun I is me

explanation.surface: Someone complains about the content of a piece of writing they dislike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I object' reads as a protest, but means the grammatical object form of I.
explanation.definitionFit: The topic a piece of writing or speech deals with is its subject or main idea.

clue.text: Publish The Curious Cat, perhaps

annotationWithheld.why: Publish The Curious Cat, perhaps: 'Publish' gives TRUMPET, but no reading of 'The Curious Cat, perhaps' was found that gives the same word; it may be misprinted

clue.text: Laugh after at least twelve balls go past the hole

indicators.note: after means the laugh comes behind the cricket piece

parts.note: a cricket over is six balls, so two or more overs make at least twelve
a hoot is a loud laugh

explanation.surface: A golfer laughs after long play when the putt runs beyond the cup.
explanation.walkthrough: An over in cricket is six deliveries, so the plural is at least twelve balls.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf a putt that runs too far beyond the cup has gone further than intended.

clue.text: Time to think logically about mutiny

parts.note: to reason is to think logically

explanation.surface: A captain takes time to think things through about a revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is a link between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rising against one's lawful ruler or commander is betrayal of the state.

clue.text: Still in one piece the day after ones's caught by ace

indicators.note: after means the day piece comes behind the rest

parts.note: 'uns is a dialect form of ones, as in 'young 'uns'
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone comes through a battering intact, the day after being caught by a star player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like an adverb of time; here it introduces the definition, meaning yet unharmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being undamaged or uninjured means coming through without harm.

clue.text: One thing on which I stand up

parts.note: a means one
people stand on their feet

explanation.surface: Something holds me upright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' means happening, as in 'what's up?'
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is going on or under way is in progress.

clue.text: Tips of the French politicians

parts.note: du means of the in French
MPs are Members of Parliament

explanation.surface: Advice given by French politicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' looks like advice but means rubbish heaps.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip in Britain is a place for rubbish, a refuse heap.

clue.text: Public character's figure of speech

explanation.surface: A public figure is known for a turn of phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A public persona is someone's image, and a metaphor or simile is an image in rhetoric.

clue.text: Couple needed to get round?

parts.note: reads like a pair of people needed to visit, but is the two-legged instrument for drawing circles

explanation.surface: Two people are required to make the rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: A drawing compass has two legs hinged together, which is why it is called a pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawing instruments with two hinged legs trace circles, which is going round.

clue.text: Fight! It's time for Western support

indicators.note: it's T for W means one letter takes the other's place

parts.note: to wrestle is to fight at close quarters

explanation.surface: A referee calls the start of a bout in a cowboy saloon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fight!' looks like a call to arms; take WRESTLE and put T in place of W.
explanation.definitionFit: A trestle is a frame of legs and a crossbar that holds up a table top.

clue.text: Abominable woman's new figure

indicators.note: abominable means dreadful, so the letters are badly mangled into a new order

parts.note: the letters of the word with the S of the possessive kept

explanation.surface: A terrible woman's latest look is not flattering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abominable' brings to mind the Yeti; it signals rearranging WOMANS into SNOWMA, and N closes the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A snowman is a figure built out of packed snow.
